slides.notes:
The engineering context
CML3112, Week 3, slide 4

Explanation to give
Use a room or floor as the physical reference. Length and width are distances in metres. Multiplying them produces area in m²; multiplying by thickness produces volume in m³.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For the displayed rectangle, 5 m × 3 m = 15 m². Density connects volume to mass. Indoor temperature, energy and cooling load are different quantities and should retain their own units.

Misconception to address
The later assignment uses slab_mass(area_m2, thickness_m). Explain its two inputs before introducing density. A number without its unit can be ambiguous.

Start with numbers and values

slides.title: Start with numbers and values

concepts.meaning: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.notes:
Start with numbers and values
CML3112, Week 3, slide 5

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

Misconception to address
A decimal point does not supply a unit. Read the variable suffix, axis label or task definition before calculating.

On this slide
Number: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
Value and unit: A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.title: Words we will use

concepts.meaning: A name referring to a value. In length_m = 5, the right side is evaluated and assigned to length_m.
int represents whole numbers; float represents approximate real numbers such as 2.5; str is text in quotes; bool is True or False.

slides.notes:
Words we will use
CML3112, Week 3, slide 6

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
length_m = 4 makes length_m refer to 4. length_m = 6 replaces that association. Printing length_m now displays 6; the name does not remember a history of both values.

Misconception to address
Changing text in a notebook cell changes the instructions. The runtime value changes only when that cell executes.

slides.sequence_source: A variable refers to its current value #1

slides.title: Python values have types
slides.caption: 3.5 + 2 gives 5.5. "3.5" + "2" joins text into "3.52".
slides.notes:
Python values have types
CML3112, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

On this slide
Type | Example | Meaning
int | 3 | Whole number
float | 3.5 | Decimal approximation
str | "3.5" | Text in quotes
bool | True / False | Logical value
NoneType | None | No value supplied
3.5 + 2 gives 5.5. "3.5" + "2" joins text into "3.52".

slides.title: Operator

concepts.meaning: A symbol for an operation: + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies, / divides, ** raises to a power. // floors a quotient, so -5 // 2 is -3.

slides.notes:
Operator
CML3112, Week 3, slide 9

Explanation to give
Translate the familiar written arithmetic signs into keyboard characters. Addition and subtraction look familiar; multiplication uses * and division uses /. Explain each operation on two small numbers before discussing variables.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 8 and 2: 8 + 2 is 10, 8 - 2 is 6, 8 * 2 is 16, and 8 / 2 is 4.0. Python 3 division produces a floating-point result even here.

Misconception to address
The letter x and the printed multiplication sign × are not Python's multiplication operator. Division by zero raises an error.

Read a function call before using it

slides.title: Read a function call before using it

concepts.meaning: Python already provides tools such as print, type and float. A function call asks a named tool to do its work: print(3) displays 3.
Parentheses hold the inputs to a call. Quotes make text: "3.5" is text; float("3.5") converts it to a number. # starts a comment that Python does not run.

slides.notes:
Read a function call before using it
CML3112, Week 3, slide 10

Explanation to give
A function call asks an existing tool to do a job. Read its name first, then the values between parentheses. The comma separates inputs when more than one is supplied. The returned result can become input to another call.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
In print(float("4.5")), the inner float call converts text to 4.5, then print displays it. In print("length", 4), print receives two inputs and normally separates them with a space.

Misconception to address
Parentheses used for a call differ from parentheses used only to group arithmetic. Identify the preceding function name.

On this slide

Parentheses, quotes and comments: Parentheses hold the inputs to a call. Quotes make text: "3.5" is text; float("3.5") converts it to a number. # starts a comment that Python does not run.

Reading Python symbols
CML3112, Week 3, slide 11

Explanation to give
Separate a value-producing expression from the instruction that uses it. Evaluate the calculation first, assign it second, and display it only if a print call asks for output. Explain parentheses, quotes and the comment symbol when pointing to them.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Do not read = and == interchangeably. A bare assignment normally produces no printed line in a notebook.

Floor division remainder and powers

slides.title: Floor division remainder and powers
slides.caption: 7 contains three groups of 2 with 1 left over: 7 = 3 × 2 + 1.
slides.notes:
Floor division remainder and powers
CML3112, Week 3, slide 17

Explanation to give
Explain // as taking the floor of a quotient, % as the remainder and ** as repeated multiplication for a positive integer exponent. “Floor” means the greatest integer no larger than the quotient.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
9 = 2 × 4 + 1, so 9 // 4 is 2 and 9 % 4 is 1. 3 ** 2 is 9. For a negative example, -9 / 4 is -2.25, so -9 // 4 is -3.

Misconception to address
% does not mean percentage. To turn 60% into a fraction, use 60 / 100. Negative floor division does not simply remove the decimal digits.

On this slide
Operator | Meaning | Example and result
// | Floor the quotient | 7 // 2 gives 3
% | Remainder | 7 % 2 gives 1
** | Raise to a power | 2 ** 3 gives 8
7 contains three groups of 2 with 1 left over: 7 = 3 × 2 + 1.

Reading powers signs and remainders

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

Which operation happens first

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.
slides.notes:
Which operation happens first
CML3112, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

Assigning and updating a named value

slides.title: Assigning and updating a named value
slides.body:
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.
slides.notes:
Assigning and updating a named value
CML3112, Week 3, slide 23

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.
slides.notes:
Numbers text and conversion

Explanation to give

4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Arithmetic that needs care

slides.title: Arithmetic that needs care
slides.body:
Parentheses run first: (2 + 4) / 2 is 3.0. Without them, division runs before addition: 2 + 4 / 2 is 4.0.

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.
slides.notes:
Arithmetic that needs care
CML3112, Week 3, slide 27

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.

Misconception to address
Indentation is part of the program, not decoration. Moving the last print four spaces right changes which path can execute it.

slides.notes:
List and index
CML3112, Week 4, slide 5

Explanation to give
A list is an ordered collection. Draw labelled positions 0, 1 and 2 above three values. The position is the address, not the value stored there. A list may contain repeated values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For [2, 4, 6], position 0 contains 2 and position 2 contains 6. len returns 3. There is no position 3. append(8) adds a new final item and the count becomes 4.

Misconception to address
Square brackets create a list when enclosing values, but select an item when placed after its name. Python counts list positions from zero.

A loop repeats instructions

slides.title: A loop repeats instructions
slides.body:
A loop runs a block more than once. One execution of the block is called an iteration.

for takes one item at a time from a collection. Use it when each item needs the same action.

while repeats while a condition stays True. Use it when a condition controls repetition.
slides.notes:
A loop repeats instructions
CML3112, Week 4, slide 10

Explanation to give
Read for item in values as “take one value, call it item, execute the indented body, then take the next value”. The loop name temporarily refers to the current item.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For values [2, 4, 6], print(item) produces 2, then 4, then 6. With count initially zero and one increment per visit, the final count is 3.

Misconception to address
The loop variable does not refer to the whole list. A statement after the indentation ends runs after the loop, not once per item.

Read every part of a for header

slides.title: Read every part of a for header
slides.body:
In for reading in readings:, for introduces repetition, reading names the current item, and readings is the collection to visit.

in connects the current-item name to that collection. The colon begins the loop body. Four spaces mark each instruction that repeats.

reading is a name we choose; it is assigned the next item automatically. It is not the same name as readings. After the last item, execution leaves the loop.

Updating a counter inside a loop

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.
slides.notes:
Updating a counter inside a loop
CML3112, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

slides.notes:
Accumulator
CML3112, Week 4, slide 16

Explanation to give
An accumulator keeps the result built so far. Initialise total before the loop, add the current reading during each visit, and calculate the mean only after all readings have been counted.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For [2, 4, 6], total changes 0 to 2 to 6 to 12. The count is 3, so the mean is 12 / 3 = 4.0. sum, len, min and max report 12, 3, 2 and 6.

Misconception to address
An empty list has count zero, so dividing by its count fails. The issued task must define the empty-data behaviour; do not silently invent a reading.

continue skips the rest of the current iteration, then starts the next iteration. It does not end the whole loop.

slides.title: A bar chart and a histogram count different things
slides.body:
A bar chart has named groups. bar(["A", "B"], [13, 16]) makes one bar for each supplied group value.

A histogram divides a numeric range into intervals called bins. hist(readings, bins=2) counts readings in two intervals.

With [12, 14, 13, 18], the intervals run from 12 to 15 and 15 to 18. Counts are 3 and 1; the final interval includes the last endpoint.

slides.title: Read a list comprehension after the full loop
slides.body:
A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.
slides.notes:

A fitted line is a numerical rule
slides.caption: Invented numbers for learning.

slides.title: A fitted line is a numerical rule
slides.body:
For these invented observations, target = 2 × input + 10 matches all four points. 2 is the slope; 10 is the intercept, the value at input zero.

A prediction error is the difference between a prediction and the measured answer. A vertical gap in the picture shows that error.

Fitting chooses the slope and intercept to minimise summed squared errors. Squaring means multiplying an error by itself; a small training error still needs an unseen-data check.
slides.notes:
A fitted line is a numerical rule
CML3112, Week 8, slide 11

Explanation to give
A fitted straight line summarises how the target changes with an input in the training examples. Its slope is the change in prediction per unit increase of input; its intercept is the prediction at input zero.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
The teaching data [1,2,3,4] and [12,14,16,18] follow y = 10 + 2x. At x = 2.5 the line predicts 15. That is an illustration, not evidence of accuracy on engineering measurements.

Misconception to address
Fitting a neat line does not establish causation. Extrapolating beyond the observed range can be unreliable.

concepts.meaning: An imputer fills missing feature values using a stated rule. Fit learns the replacement from training observations only. Prediction reuses that stored replacement.

CML3112, Week 8, slide 33

Explanation to give
A pipeline keeps preparation and prediction in one ordered procedure. Fit learns preparation values from training data and then fits the model. Prediction reuses those saved values.

slides.title: MAE and RMSE

concepts.meaning: MAE averages absolute prediction errors. RMSE squares errors, averages them and takes the square root. Both use target units. RMSE is more sensitive to large errors.

slides.notes:
MAE and RMSE
CML3112, Week 8, slide 41

Explanation to give
Match each prediction with the actual value for the same observation. MAE averages error magnitudes. RMSE averages squared errors and then takes the square root, restoring the target unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Actual [10,20] and predicted [12,16] have differences -2 and 4. MAE is (2+4)/2 = 3. RMSE is sqrt((4+16)/2) = sqrt(10), about 3.1623.

Misconception to address
Signed errors can cancel if simply averaged. MAE is not a plus/minus guarantee for every case, and RMSE is not in squared units after the square root.

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:
R² compares squared errors with predicting the mean of the evaluated targets. It is a score, not “percentage accuracy”.

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

Precision / Recall
CML3112, Week 9, slide 11

Explanation to give
Use two different denominators. Precision looks only at issued warnings. Recall looks only at real cases that needed a warning. Say the population in the denominator before calculating.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If TP=3, FP=1 and FN=2, precision is 3/(3+1)=0.75 and recall is 3/(3+2)=0.60. One asks whether warnings are reliable; the other asks whether true problems were found.

Misconception to address
The denominators are not interchangeable. Follow the published convention when a denominator is zero and explain why that case arises.

slides.sequence_source: A category can become indicator columns #1

slides.title: Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.
slides.notes:
Accuracy can hide missed warnings
CML3112, Week 9, slide 28

Explanation to give
Accuracy counts all correct classifications together. In an imbalanced dataset, correct majority-class answers can dominate the score while the minority class is consistently missed.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 95 normal cases and 5 genuine faults, always predicting normal gives 95% accuracy but detects zero faults. Fault recall is zero.

Misconception to address
A high headline accuracy alone is insufficient for a warning system. Report the confusion counts and the relevant costs.

slides.title: Parameters hyperparameters and a fold
slides.body:
A parameter is learned during fitting, such as a line’s slope. A hyperparameter is a setting chosen around fitting, such as a tree’s max_depth.

A fold is one part of the development data used for a validation turn. Refit the entire preprocessing and model on the other parts for that turn.

Compare candidate settings using validation evidence. Keep the final test outside that selection process.
slides.notes:
Parameters hyperparameters and a fold
CML3112, Week 10, slide 19

Explanation to give
A parameter is learned during fit. A hyperparameter is chosen as a setting. Cross-validation repeats fitting with different held-out portions of the development data to assess choices more steadily.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If validation errors are 2, 3 and 4, the mean is 3. Their spread indicates sensitivity to the held-out portion. A standard deviation describes that spread; it is not automatically a confidence interval.

Misconception to address
Fit preprocessing separately within each training fold. Keep groups or time order intact where required. The final test remains separate from tuning.

Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

slides.body:
Each row contains two inputs. for a, b in rows: assigns them to a and b. [a, b, a * b] builds a new row with their product as a third input.

For row [2, 3], append [2, 3, 6]. For row [4, 5], append [4, 5, 20]. The function returns the newly built list of rows.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]
y = [3, 5, 5, 8, 8]
validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]
truth = [4, 6]
def with_interaction(rows):
    result = []
    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression()
base.fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression()
extended.fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)
print(round(base_error, 6))
validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.
slides.notes:
Scaling changes units of comparison
CML3112, Week 11, slide 22

Explanation to give
Scaling changes numerical ranges to make inputs comparable for algorithms that are sensitive to magnitude. Learn the scaling values from the training subset and apply the same transformation later.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Converting a length from metres to millimetres multiplies its numeric value by 1000 without changing the physical length. Standardisation uses training mean and standard deviation to express relative position.

Misconception to address
Scaling is not evidence that all features are equally useful. Never learn the scaler separately on validation or test observations.

Encoding and Scaling
CML3112, Week 11, slide 23

Explanation to give
One-hot encoding gives each category its own indicator column. A row has a 1 in the column matching its category and 0 in the others.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For categories A and B, an A row becomes [1,0] and a B row becomes [0,1]. Assigning A=1 and B=2 could accidentally suggest a meaningful numerical distance or order.

Misconception to address
Fit the encoder on training data and define how to handle categories not seen during training. Do not invent an ordinal meaning for names.

slides.notes:
Start with numbers and values
CML3113, Week 2, slide 14

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

Misconception to address
A decimal point does not supply a unit. Read the variable suffix, axis label or task definition before calculating.

Give a value a name

slides.title: Give a value a name

concepts.meaning: A variable is a name referring to a value. In readings = 12, readings is the name and 12 is its initial number.
Read = as “assign”, not “is equal to”. Python calculates the right side first, then gives that value to the name on the left. A later assignment replaces its previous value.

slides.notes:
Give a value a name
CML3113, Week 2, slide 15

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
length_m = 4 makes length_m refer to 4. length_m = 6 replaces that association. Printing length_m now displays 6; the name does not remember a history of both values.

Misconception to address
Changing text in a notebook cell changes the instructions. The runtime value changes only when that cell executes.

The words in the repair exercises
CML3113, Week 2, slide 27

Explanation to give
Teach a diagnosis sequence: read the final error line, locate the indicated instruction, compare the expected input with what actually exists, and fix the first cause. Explain the error type rather than treating all red output alike.

slides.title: Start with numbers and values

concepts.meaning: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.notes:
Start with numbers and values
CML3113, Week 3, slide 5

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

Misconception to address
A decimal point does not supply a unit. Read the variable suffix, axis label or task definition before calculating.

Value and unit: A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.title: Words we will use

concepts.meaning: A name referring to a value. In length_m = 5, the right side is evaluated and assigned to length_m.
int represents whole numbers; float represents approximate real numbers such as 2.5; str is text in quotes; bool is True or False.

slides.notes:
Words we will use
CML3113, Week 3, slide 6

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Misconception to address
Changing text in a notebook cell changes the instructions. The runtime value changes only when that cell executes.

slides.notes:
Python values have types
CML3113, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

On this slide

int | 3 | Whole number
float | 3.5 | Decimal approximation
str | "3.5" | Text in quotes
bool | True / False | Logical value
NoneType | None | No value supplied

Translate the familiar written arithmetic signs into keyboard characters. Addition and subtraction look familiar; multiplication uses * and division uses /. Explain each operation on two small numbers before discussing variables.

Explanation to give
Explain // as taking the floor of a quotient, % as the remainder and ** as repeated multiplication for a positive integer exponent. “Floor” means the greatest integer no larger than the quotient.

% | Remainder | 7 % 2 gives 1
** | Raise to a power | 2 ** 3 gives 8

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

Which operation happens first

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.
slides.notes:
Which operation happens first
CML3113, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

Assigning and updating a named value

slides.title: Assigning and updating a named value
slides.body:
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.
slides.notes:
Assigning and updating a named value
CML3113, Week 3, slide 23

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

Numbers text and conversion

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.
slides.notes:
Numbers text and conversion
CML3113, Week 3, slide 25

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

30 >= 30 asks “Is 30 at least 30?” The answer is True. 28 >= 30 gives False.

True and False have type bool. "False" is text, not the Boolean value False. Conditions use Boolean results to choose what happens next.

A condition and an if block

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.
slides.notes:
A condition and an if block
CML3113, Week 3, slide 36

Explanation to give
Explain an if block as a gate. Python evaluates the condition once when it reaches the header. If True, it executes the indented statements; otherwise it skips them. The colon introduces the block.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For reading = 28 and a condition reading >= 30, the “warm” line is skipped. The unindented “check finished” line still runs. At 30, both lines run.

Misconception to address
Indentation is part of the program, not decoration. Moving the last print four spaces right changes which path can execute it.

On this slide
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.

slides.title: A loop repeats instructions
slides.body:
A loop runs a block more than once. One execution of the block is called an iteration.

for takes one item at a time from a collection. Use it when each item needs the same action.

while repeats while a condition stays True. Use it when a condition controls repetition.

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.

Misconception to address

A while loop checks before each repetition

slides.title: A while loop checks before each repetition
slides.body:
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.
slides.notes:
A while loop checks before each repetition

Misconception to address
If count is never updated, the condition stays True. Interrupt a stuck runtime rather than waiting indefinitely, then identify the missing update.

continue and break change a loop’s path

slides.title: continue and break change a loop’s path
slides.body:
continue skips the rest of the current iteration, then starts the next iteration. It does not end the whole loop.

break exits the nearest enclosing loop immediately. Execution resumes after that loop.

Put the condition inside the loop with four spaces. Its action is inside that condition with eight spaces: an indented block inside another block.
slides.notes:
continue and break change a loop’s path

Explanation to give
continue ends the current iteration and proceeds to the next item. break ends the nearest enclosing loop completely. Trace the same data twice to show the distinction.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Over [1, 2, 3], skipping 2 with continue still allows 3 to be processed. Breaking when 2 is reached prevents both 2's remaining work and the later visit to 3.

Misconception to address
Statements below continue or break in that iteration are skipped. Neither word means “restart the whole notebook”.

slides.body:
record = {"unit": "A", "reading": 4} stores two key–value pairs. Keys name fields; values hold the information.

Braces enclose the dictionary. A colon separates each key from its value and a comma separates pairs. Each key is unique.

Tuples and unpacking

slides.title: Tuples and unpacking
slides.body:
A tuple stores items in order. point = (2, 3) stores two coordinates; point[0] is 2. You cannot reassign point[0].

x, y = point gives the first item to x and the second to y. This is unpacking; the number of names must match the number of items.

A tuple prevents replacing its positions. It does not freeze the contents of a mutable object stored inside it.

A set remembers distinct items

slides.title: A set remembers distinct items
slides.body:
A set is useful when the question is “Have we seen this ID?” It keeps one instance of each distinct item.

seen = set() creates an empty set. seen.add("A") adds an item. "A" in seen asks whether it is present.

Do not use a set when position or repeated readings matter. Sets cannot be indexed. {} creates an empty dictionary, not an empty set.
slides.notes:
A set remembers distinct items
CML3113, Week 4, slide 41

Explanation to give
A set answers whether an item is present and stores each distinct item once. It has no numeric positions. Use it to remember IDs already encountered.

Misconception to address
{} creates an empty dictionary. Use set() for an empty set. Sets are unsuitable when duplicate measurements or a particular order must be retained.

slides.caption: Choose by the question: ordered readings, named fields, fixed positions, or distinct IDs.
slides.notes:
How the four collections differ
CML3113, Week 4, slide 43

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

slides.notes:
Raw data and Missing value
CML3113, Week 6, slide 5

Explanation to give
Raw data is the original record of what was received. Work on a copy and record changes. Missing means unrecorded; zero may be a valid reading. An unusual value is a reason to investigate, not automatic permission to delete.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
A temperature sensor can genuinely report zero degrees. A blank temperature conveys no reading. Treating both as zero would change the mean and disguise missingness.

Misconception to address

slides.title: Read a list comprehension after the full loop
slides.body:
A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.
slides.notes:

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
squares = [x * x for x in [2, 3]] means initialise an empty list, take 2 then 3, and append each square. The result is [4, 9].

Misconception to address
This syntax is optional for these beginner tasks. A clear full loop is acceptable when it returns the required result.

slides.title: A fitted line is a numerical rule
slides.body:
For these invented observations, target = 2 × input + 10 matches all four points. 2 is the slope; 10 is the intercept, the value at input zero.

A prediction error is the difference between a prediction and the measured answer. A vertical gap in the picture shows that error.

Fitting chooses the slope and intercept to minimise summed squared errors. Squaring means multiplying an error by itself; a small training error still needs an unseen-data check.
slides.notes:
A fitted line is a numerical rule
CML3113, Week 8, slide 11

Explanation to give
A fitted straight line summarises how the target changes with an input in the training examples. Its slope is the change in prediction per unit increase of input; its intercept is the prediction at input zero.

Fitting a neat line does not establish causation. Extrapolating beyond the observed range can be unreliable.

slides.title: A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers
slides.body:
A matrix has rows and columns. For modelling, one row is one observation and each column is one input feature.

[[1, 20], [2, 22]] has two rows and two columns. The outer list contains rows; each inner list contains that row’s features.

X is a conventional name for this input table. y holds one known target per row. These names have no special power in Python.
slides.notes:

Explanation to give

Misconception to address
Swapping feature columns changes their meaning even if dimensions still match. The model expects the same order and units at prediction time.

Explanation to give
A pipeline keeps preparation and prediction in one ordered procedure. Fit learns preparation values from training data and then fits the model. Prediction reuses those saved values.

slides.title: MAE and RMSE

concepts.meaning: MAE averages absolute prediction errors. RMSE squares errors, averages them and takes the square root. Both use target units. RMSE is more sensitive to large errors.

slides.notes:
MAE and RMSE
CML3113, Week 8, slide 41

Explanation to give
Match each prediction with the actual value for the same observation. MAE averages error magnitudes. RMSE averages squared errors and then takes the square root, restoring the target unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Actual [10,20] and predicted [12,16] have differences -2 and 4. MAE is (2+4)/2 = 3. RMSE is sqrt((4+16)/2) = sqrt(10), about 3.1623.

Misconception to address
Signed errors can cancel if simply averaged. MAE is not a plus/minus guarantee for every case, and RMSE is not in squared units after the square root.

On this slide

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:
R² compares squared errors with predicting the mean of the evaluated targets. It is a score, not “percentage accuracy”.

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

Explanation to give

Probability and a decision threshold
CML3113, Week 9, slide 13

Explanation to give
A probability-like score becomes a class decision only after choosing a threshold. The threshold expresses an operating trade-off; an error-cost rule states which mistakes matter more for this task.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.
slides.notes:
Accuracy can hide missed warnings
CML3113, Week 9, slide 28

Explanation to give
Accuracy counts all correct classifications together. In an imbalanced dataset, correct majority-class answers can dominate the score while the minority class is consistently missed.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 95 normal cases and 5 genuine faults, always predicting normal gives 95% accuracy but detects zero faults. Fault recall is zero.

Misconception to address
A high headline accuracy alone is insufficient for a warning system. Report the confusion counts and the relevant costs.

slides.notes:
Category predictions and operating thresholds
CML3113, Week 9, slide 32

Explanation to give
A probability-like score becomes a class decision only after choosing a threshold. The threshold expresses an operating trade-off; an error-cost rule states which mistakes matter more for this task.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
At threshold >= 0.6, scores 0.59 and 0.60 give 0 and 1. Lowering the threshold usually raises more warnings, potentially reducing misses while increasing false alarms.

Misconception to address
A score of 0.8 is not a guarantee that this particular prediction is right. Evaluate calibration if probabilities will be interpreted literally. Costs must come from the stated scenario.

concepts.meaning: Performance on new cases from the intended setting, not merely on records already used.
Overfitting captures training-specific detail that fails to transfer. Underfitting misses useful patterns. Score gaps are clues, not a complete diagnosis.

slides.notes:
Generalisation and Overfitting and underfitting
CML3113, Week 10, slide 7

Explanation to give
Generalisation means working on relevant observations not used to learn the model. Overfitting captures training-specific detail; underfitting misses useful structure even in training.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
A very deep tree may memorise noisy training readings. A constant baseline may miss a clear trend. Compare training and validation errors to diagnose these possibilities.

Misconception to address
A gap between errors is evidence to investigate, not proof of one cause. Check whether the evaluation data actually represents future use.

slides.title: Leakage and Group split

concepts.meaning: Information enters model development that would not legitimately be available, such as the answer or information from evaluation rows.
Keep all observations from the same equipment in one partition when the goal is prediction for unseen equipment.

slides.notes:
Leakage and Group split
CML3113, Week 10, slide 8

Explanation to give
If the intended use is new equipment, keep all observations from each equipment ID together in one partition. Otherwise near-related records can make evaluation look easier than deployment.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Equipment A recorded on Monday and Tuesday belongs in one partition under a group split. Splitting those two rows across train and validation lets the model see the same equipment on both sides.

Misconception to address
Different record IDs do not guarantee independent equipment. For forecasting, chronology may be the key constraint instead; choose the split to match the stated use.

concepts.meaning: Preprocessing changes inputs, for example filling missing values. A pipeline fits these steps on training data and applies the same fitted changes to new inputs.

slides.notes:
Preprocessing and pipeline
CML3113, Week 10, slide 14

Explanation to give
A pipeline keeps preparation and prediction in one ordered procedure. Fit learns preparation values from training data and then fits the model. Prediction reuses those saved values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For training feature values 20, 22, missing and 24, the learned median is 22. A missing value in a new observation also receives 22, without recalculating from the new observations.

Misconception to address
Filling all records before splitting leaks information. A pipeline avoids that only when its fit receives the correct training subset.

A ratio divides quantities; an interaction multiplies them. Both need a domain explanation and a unit check.

slides.notes:
Derived feature and Ratio and interaction
CML3113, Week 11, slide 6

Explanation to give
A derived feature is a new input calculated from known inputs. Explain its physical or operational reason and its units before presenting it to a model. An interaction allows one input's effect to depend on another.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For load_pct 50 and ambient_c 30, the course interaction load_pct * ambient_c is 1500. Separately, load_pct / 100 gives the fraction 0.5. These are different derived quantities. The interaction is a hypothesis to test, not a measured law.

Misconception to address
A plausible physical story does not guarantee an improvement. Do not use the target or information that would only become available after the prediction.

On this slide
Derived feature: A new input calculated from existing inputs. Its definition and unit must be stated.
Ratio and interaction: A ratio divides quantities; an interaction multiplies them. Both need a domain explanation and a unit check.

slides.title: Read the physical example across programmes
slides.body:
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.

slides.title: Ablation and Improvement

concepts.meaning: Compare a model with and without a feature while keeping the data partitions, model family and metric fixed.
For an error metric, baseline error minus new error. A negative result means the added feature worsened validation error in that comparison.

slides.notes:
Ablation and Improvement
CML3113, Week 11, slide 12

Explanation to give
An ablation comparison changes one feature or component while holding the evaluation protocol fixed. This helps attribute any observed difference to the change being tested.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If validation MAE drops from 5 to 4, the absolute reduction is 1 in the target unit and the relative reduction is 20%. If it rises, the extra feature has not helped under this protocol.

Misconception to address
Changing the split, model and feature at once makes attribution unclear. Use the same observations, metric and fitting rules for both variants.

On this slide
Ablation: Compare a model with and without a feature while keeping the data partitions, model family and metric fixed.
Improvement: For an error metric, baseline error minus new error. A negative result means the added feature worsened validation error in that comparison.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]

validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]

slides.practice_code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]
y = [3, 5, 5, 8, 8]
validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]
truth = [4, 6]
def with_interaction(rows):
    result = []
    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression()
base.fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression()
extended.fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)
print(round(base_error, 6))
validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.
slides.notes:
Scaling changes units of comparison
CML3113, Week 11, slide 22

Explanation to give
Scaling changes numerical ranges to make inputs comparable for algorithms that are sensitive to magnitude. Learn the scaling values from the training subset and apply the same transformation later.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Converting a length from metres to millimetres multiplies its numeric value by 1000 without changing the physical length. Standardisation uses training mean and standard deviation to express relative position.

Misconception to address
Scaling is not evidence that all features are equally useful. Never learn the scaler separately on validation or test observations.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.

slides.title: Encoding and Scaling

concepts.meaning: Representing a category numerically. One-hot uses separate indicator columns. Arbitrary integer labels can falsely suggest an order.
Changing the numerical scale of features. Fit learned scaling on training data only. It matters for distance-based models but is not required by ordinary decision trees.

slides.notes:
Encoding and Scaling
CML3113, Week 11, slide 23

Explanation to give
One-hot encoding gives each category its own indicator column. A row has a 1 in the column matching its category and 0 in the others.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For categories A and B, an A row becomes [1,0] and a B row becomes [0,1]. Assigning A=1 and B=2 could accidentally suggest a meaningful numerical distance or order.

Misconception to address
Fit the encoder on training data and define how to handle categories not seen during training. Do not invent an ordinal meaning for names.

On this slide
Encoding: Representing a category numerically. One-hot uses separate indicator columns. Arbitrary integer labels can falsely suggest an order.
Scaling: Changing the numerical scale of features. Fit learned scaling on training data only. It matters for distance-based models but is not required by ordinary decision trees.

Rescaling an input usually does not change the partitions available to an ordinary decision tree.

An identifier or a future-known field can create an apparent improvement without useful predictive information.

Dividing by zero can produce infinity or an error; decide what the denominator means before replacing it.
slides.notes:
Features without misleading evaluation
CML3113, Week 11, slide 26

Explanation to give
An ablation comparison changes one feature or component while holding the evaluation protocol fixed. This helps attribute any observed difference to the change being tested.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If validation MAE drops from 5 to 4, the absolute reduction is 1 in the target unit and the relative reduction is 20%. If it rises, the extra feature has not helped under this protocol.

Misconception to address
Changing the split, model and feature at once makes attribution unclear. Use the same observations, metric and fitting rules for both variants.

concepts.meaning: A condition a candidate must satisfy, such as MAE at most 3 and latency at most 10 ms.
Time taken to produce a prediction under stated measurement conditions. Hardware and measurement method matter.

slides.notes:
Constraint and Latency
CML3113, Week 12, slide 5

Explanation to give
Separate eligibility from ranking. A model that violates a required error or latency limit cannot win merely because another score is attractive. Latency is time per prediction in the stated measurement setting.

concepts.meaning: A variable is a name referring to a value. In readings = 12, readings is the name and 12 is its initial number.

slides.notes:
Give a value a name
CML3111, Week 2, slide 15

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Python values have types
CML3111, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

slides.title: Read a function call before using it

concepts.meaning: Python already provides tools such as print, type and float. A function call asks a named tool to do its work: print(3) displays 3.

slides.title: Reading Python symbols
slides.body:

Which operation happens first

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.
slides.notes:
Which operation happens first
CML3111, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

slides.title: Assigning and updating a named value
slides.body:
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.
slides.notes:
Assigning and updating a named value
CML3111, Week 3, slide 23

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.
slides.notes:
Numbers text and conversion
CML3111, Week 3, slide 25

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.

slides.title: None means there is no result value
slides.body:
None is a Python value used here to mean “no calculated answer”. It is not zero, an empty string, or the word "None".

A function returns None explicitly with return None. A function also returns None if it reaches its end without a return value.

A caller must handle None before trying arithmetic with the result. The next example returns it for division by zero.
slides.notes:
None means there is no result value

Misconception to address
A function that reaches its end without a return value also returns None. None is a real Python value, not the text "None" or the number zero.

slides.title: One value and a collection of values
slides.body:
A variable can refer to one value: reading = 98. A collection stores several related values under one name.

Python has several collection types. Choose one according to how you need to find, change or organise its contents.
slides.notes:
One value and a collection of values
CML3111, Week 3, slide 63

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

An index is an item’s position. Python starts counting at zero: readings[0] is 98, readings[1] is 105, readings[2] is 92.

Updating a counter inside a loop

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.
slides.notes:
Updating a counter inside a loop
CML3111, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

A while loop checks before each repetition

slides.title: A while loop checks before each repetition
slides.body:
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.
slides.notes:
A while loop checks before each repetition

Misconception to address
If count is never updated, the condition stays True. Interrupt a stuck runtime rather than waiting indefinitely, then identify the missing update.

range supplies a sequence of integers

slides.title: range supplies a sequence of integers
slides.body:
range(3) supplies 0, 1 and 2. The stop value 3 is excluded. range(1, 4) supplies 1, 2 and 3.

Use range with for when a numbered repetition is useful. The loop still works by taking the next supplied item.

range(0, 6, 2) uses a step of 2 and supplies 0, 2, 4. A step is the change between successive numbers; it cannot be zero.
slides.notes:
range supplies a sequence of integers
CML3111, Week 4, slide 30

Explanation to give
range supplies integers in order. Its stop value is excluded. Say the sequence out loud before executing the loop so the boundary is visible.

continue skips the rest of the current iteration, then starts the next iteration. It does not end the whole loop.

slides.title: Tuples and unpacking
slides.body:
A tuple stores items in order. point = (2, 3) stores two coordinates; point[0] is 2. You cannot reassign point[0].

x, y = point gives the first item to x and the second to y. This is unpacking; the number of names must match the number of items.

A tuple prevents replacing its positions. It does not freeze the contents of a mutable object stored inside it.

slides.title: A set remembers distinct items

A set is useful when the question is “Have we seen this ID?” It keeps one instance of each distinct item.

seen = set() creates an empty set. seen.add("A") adds an item. "A" in seen asks whether it is present.

Raw data and Missing value
CML3111, Week 6, slide 5

Explanation to give
Raw data is the original record of what was received. Work on a copy and record changes. Missing means unrecorded; zero may be a valid reading. An unusual value is a reason to investigate, not automatic permission to delete.

Record and equipment ID and Median and imputation
CML3111, Week 6, slide 6

Explanation to give
Sort the observed numbers to find the median. For an odd count use the middle number; for an even count average the two middle numbers. Imputation inserts an estimate for a missing value and should be recorded as an estimate.

A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.
slides.notes:
Read a list comprehension after the full loop
CML3111, Week 6, slide 39

Explanation to give
A comprehension is a compact way to construct a list. First show the equivalent full loop so the learner can identify the expression, the iteration and any condition.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
squares = [x * x for x in [2, 3]] means initialise an empty list, take 2 then 3, and append each square. The result is [4, 9].

Misconception to address
This syntax is optional for these beginner tasks. A clear full loop is acceptable when it returns the required result.

Do not choose a cleaning rule merely because it makes the chart smoother. The rule must follow the task and the measurement context.

concepts.meaning: An imputer fills missing feature values using a stated rule. Fit learns the replacement from training observations only. Prediction reuses that stored replacement.
A pipeline connects preprocessing and a model. make_pipeline creates that connection. Its fit learns both stages on training data; predict applies them to new features.

slides.notes:
Reuse the same preparation on new inputs
CML3111, Week 8, slide 33

Explanation to give
A pipeline keeps preparation and prediction in one ordered procedure. Fit learns preparation values from training data and then fits the model. Prediction reuses those saved values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For training feature values 20, 22, missing and 24, the learned median is 22. A missing value in a new observation also receives 22, without recalculating from the new observations.

Misconception to address
Filling all records before splitting leaks information. A pipeline avoids that only when its fit receives the correct training subset.

On this slide
Imputer: An imputer fills missing feature values using a stated rule. Fit learns the replacement from training observations only. Prediction reuses that stored replacement.
Pipeline: A pipeline connects preprocessing and a model. make_pipeline creates that connection. Its fit learns both stages on training data; predict applies them to new features.

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:
R² compares squared errors with predicting the mean of the evaluated targets. It is a score, not “percentage accuracy”.

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

Probability and a decision threshold
CML3111, Week 9, slide 13

Explanation to give
A probability-like score becomes a class decision only after choosing a threshold. The threshold expresses an operating trade-off; an error-cost rule states which mistakes matter more for this task.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
At threshold >= 0.6, scores 0.59 and 0.60 give 0 and 1. Lowering the threshold usually raises more warnings, potentially reducing misses while increasing false alarms.

Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.sequence_source: A category can become indicator columns #1

slides.title: Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.
slides.notes:
Accuracy can hide missed warnings
CML3111, Week 9, slide 28

Explanation to give
Accuracy counts all correct classifications together. In an imbalanced dataset, correct majority-class answers can dominate the score while the minority class is consistently missed.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 95 normal cases and 5 genuine faults, always predicting normal gives 95% accuracy but detects zero faults. Fault recall is zero.

Misconception to address
A high headline accuracy alone is insufficient for a warning system. Report the confusion counts and the relevant costs.

concepts.meaning: Performance on new cases from the intended setting, not merely on records already used.
Overfitting captures training-specific detail that fails to transfer. Underfitting misses useful patterns. Score gaps are clues, not a complete diagnosis.

slides.notes:
Generalisation and Overfitting and underfitting
CML3111, Week 10, slide 7

Explanation to give
Generalisation means working on relevant observations not used to learn the model. Overfitting captures training-specific detail; underfitting misses useful structure even in training.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
A very deep tree may memorise noisy training readings. A constant baseline may miss a clear trend. Compare training and validation errors to diagnose these possibilities.

Misconception to address
A gap between errors is evidence to investigate, not proof of one cause. Check whether the evaluation data actually represents future use.

On this slide
Generalisation: Performance on new cases from the intended setting, not merely on records already used.
Overfitting and underfitting: Overfitting captures training-specific detail that fails to transfer. Underfitting misses useful patterns. Score gaps are clues, not a complete diagnosis.

slides.notes:
Leakage and Group split
CML3111, Week 10, slide 8

Explanation to give
If the intended use is new equipment, keep all observations from each equipment ID together in one partition. Otherwise near-related records can make evaluation look easier than deployment.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Equipment A recorded on Monday and Tuesday belongs in one partition under a group split. Splitting those two rows across train and validation lets the model see the same equipment on both sides.

Misconception to address
Different record IDs do not guarantee independent equipment. For forecasting, chronology may be the key constraint instead; choose the split to match the stated use.

Preprocessing and pipeline

slides.title: Preprocessing and pipeline

concepts.meaning: Preprocessing changes inputs, for example filling missing values. A pipeline fits these steps on training data and applies the same fitted changes to new inputs.

slides.notes:
Preprocessing and pipeline
CML3111, Week 10, slide 14

Explanation to give
A pipeline keeps preparation and prediction in one ordered procedure. Fit learns preparation values from training data and then fits the model. Prediction reuses those saved values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For training feature values 20, 22, missing and 24, the learned median is 22. A missing value in a new observation also receives 22, without recalculating from the new observations.

Misconception to address
Filling all records before splitting leaks information. A pipeline avoids that only when its fit receives the correct training subset.

slides.title: Parameters hyperparameters and a fold
slides.body:
A parameter is learned during fitting, such as a line’s slope. A hyperparameter is a setting chosen around fitting, such as a tree’s max_depth.

A fold is one part of the development data used for a validation turn. Refit the entire preprocessing and model on the other parts for that turn.

Compare candidate settings using validation evidence. Keep the final test outside that selection process.
slides.notes:
Parameters hyperparameters and a fold
CML3111, Week 10, slide 19

Explanation to give
A parameter is learned during fit. A hyperparameter is chosen as a setting. Cross-validation repeats fitting with different held-out portions of the development data to assess choices more steadily.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If validation errors are 2, 3 and 4, the mean is 3. Their spread indicates sensitivity to the held-out portion. A standard deviation describes that spread; it is not automatically a confidence interval.

Misconception to address
Fit preprocessing separately within each training fold. Keep groups or time order intact where required. The final test remains separate from tuning.

slides.title: Read the physical example across programmes
slides.body:
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]

slides.practice_code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]
y = [3, 5, 5, 8, 8]
validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]
truth = [4, 6]
def with_interaction(rows):
    result = []
    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression()
base.fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression()
extended.fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)
print(round(base_error, 6))
validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.
slides.notes:
Scaling changes units of comparison
CML3111, Week 11, slide 22

Explanation to give
Scaling changes numerical ranges to make inputs comparable for algorithms that are sensitive to magnitude. Learn the scaling values from the training subset and apply the same transformation later.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Converting a length from metres to millimetres multiplies its numeric value by 1000 without changing the physical length. Standardisation uses training mean and standard deviation to express relative position.

Misconception to address
Scaling is not evidence that all features are equally useful. Never learn the scaler separately on validation or test observations.

Establish units and whether boundaries are inclusive. An error of 4 is not comparable across different target units or evaluation samples.
